I am interested in DIVALIKE and calculating the probability per node, but since this analysis (DIVALIKE) has been running for more than  20 hours and not yet finished. I will like to run the analysis using multiple trees from BEAST (Reviewer´s suggestions) and compare with the results from the standard (MCC tree) but I cannot until the DIVALIKE run is finished.  I will try the example data once the Divalike is done and hope it goes smoothly. Thanks,

Marie Claire

Hi -- the reason that DIVALIKE run is taking so long is that you are running a Maximum Likelihood analysis, but the LnL (the log of the likelihood) is coming up as NaN.  So nothing is optimizing, and it may run forever for all I know.  Surely you have seen how the LnL is supposed to increase (becomes less negative) in the runs that work??

Before I look at details, **important** point here:

The goal with BioGeoBEARS, or any analysis, not to "get it to run".  The real goal is to understand what you are doing!!!!!  The current script has this for each model:

===================
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[1]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[2]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[3]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[4]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[5]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[6]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[7]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[8]] = states_list_0based_NEW
===================

...this means you are time-stratifying the analysis, but each timeperiod has an identical list of states!  So, there is no reason to time-stratify. 

However, you get the same error with a non-time stratified analysis (lnL=-1e50 is equivalent to lnL=NaN), if the states_list is constrained.


OK, looking at your run:

1. The problem seems to be caused by the interaction between your user-constrained states_list and the DIVALIKE model. Between tips 2 and 3 (AB and BDE, tiplabels 1767 and 2359), the analysis can find no scenario that gives these tip data a nonzero probability at their common ancestor node. DEC allows subset-sympatry as well as vicariance, so it is more flexible, but DIVALIKE is vicariance-only.  This produces a NaN in the likelihood, which then produces a LnL=-1e50 under some settings.

This would be fine if it happened somewhere in the middle of the chain -- sometimes extreme parameter values get tried and result in NaN likelihoods, these are converted to -1e50 and the analysis says "Wow, that was a horrible guess at parameter values, let's try something else."  But, if even your starting parameters produce NaN, probably you've got an overly-constrained states lists.



2. I fiddled with your list of disallowed ranges:

This is what failed:
nonadjacent=c("AC","AD","AE","AF","AG","AH","BE","BG","BH","CG","CH","DF","DG","DH","EH")

This, however, worked:
nonadjacent=c("AF","AG","AH","BG","BH","CG","CH","DF","DG","DH","EH")

...however, including AD, BE, etc. as disallowed ranges caused crashes again. So, these are crucial intermediate states for explaining sister species like (AB, BDE), under the DIVALIKE model. 


3.  HAVE A SERIOUS THINK ABOUT WHY YOU ARE CONSTRAINING ALLOWED RANGES AT ALL!  For example, you have a tip range of BDE.  All that is required to turn BDE into BE is an "e" event, loss of D.  So, how can BE really be considered an impossible range?  You have allowed everything up to ranges with a size of 4 areas, so eliminating a few 2-area ranges is a bit odd.


4. I have now updated the code so that an explicit error message is produced if the initial lnL calculation fails, and the run is stopped,.  Update from GitHub to get this fix.


5. On the other issues, you should really walk before you run!  In all things, the first steps are:

5a. Take a deep breath and review your decisions...does what your script is doing make sense?

5b. Do the same for whatever a reviewer says...reviewers often suggest things because they are mildly curious, that might make no difference.


6. "I have also tried o search for nay published paper using multiple Beast trees for the Biogeo analyses. but not seen any. Do you know of any such paper."

One of them is Wood, Matzke et al. 2012, Systematic Biology -- this was before BioGeoBEARS, but it ran Lagrange on a bunch of trees.  IMHO the effort-to-reward ratio was marginal in that case, but like I say here, it will all depend on how variable the BEAST trees are compared to the MCC tree: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/M8zw8Kidseo

Cheers,
Nick

On Thursday, November 15, 2018 at 12:27:06 PM UTC+13, JP F wrote:
Hello Nick and all.

I was reading this thread and I have a question regarding the optimization/run time.

I've had in the past runs that were fast, average and slow.

What is the criteria the program uses to finish the run? How much does it need to converge/optimize? Is there a pre established criterion?

Cheers,

JP

Hi -- R has a large number of functions that do optimization (of likelihood or any other function that returns an objective that can be maximized or minimized).  There is a little world of such optimizers and math-type-people who construct them.

BioGeoBEARS allows 3 options:

optim (from default R)
optimx (from optimx R package)
GenSA (from GenSA R package)

...specifically, within each of these, a sub-algorithm is chosen that optimizes parameters within bounds (one of these is called L-BGFS-B, which if you google it you will see is an algorithm found in all sorts of implementations in various computer languages.

Each of these has a "stopping rule", which is something like "if the objective fails to improve by 0.00001 after x steps, then stop".  Sometimes the criterion is about the inferred slope of the objective (which will be 0 at the peak).  Usually there is an obscure way to change the default, but it is not trivial and requires burrowing into the original package (and sometimes the FORTRAN or C++ code underneath the R package).

Each optimizer returns a result which contains the maximized objective value, the parameters that produced this value, and some information on the search.  BioGeoBEARS just includes this whole output in the results object; to interpret it, you have to study the help for the original optimizer functions.


In general, speed works like this:

From faster to slower:
=============================
optimx with $speedup=TRUE
(the speedup=TRUE setting in BioGeoBEARS sets limits on the maximum number of iterations to search through)

optimx with $speedup=FALSE

optim

GenSA
=============================

In general, accuracy (meaning avoiding optimization failure, claiming a Max. Likelihood result that is a local optimum rather than the actual Maximum of the Likelihood) seems to work like this:
GenSA > optimx with $speedup=FALSE > optimx with $speedup=TRUE > optim

...but for most basic problems they all return the same thing.  The only place I've seen this trend matter in any reliable way is (1) very complex models (base models +x +traits etc.) or (2) weird cases with tiny datasets and 2 optima.

Therefore, if you have a particularly complex model, or just are worried, use GenSA (but it may take 2-10 times as long). 

Regardless, no optimizer is perfect, these are just hill-climbing algorithms of various sorts.  Advice:

ML optimization routines and their pitfalls
http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#ML_optimx


OTHER INFLUENCES ON RUN TIME

In addition to the optimizer, the run time will be influenced by many other things:

More areas = more states/ranges = slower matrix exponentiation = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run
More free parameters = bigger parameter space to search through = slower overall run
Slower/older computer = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run
Fewer cores / not using the multiple cores (R in Mac Terminal can do multicores, R.app cannot) = slower overall run

Cheers,
Nick

BioGeoBEARS allows 3 options:

optim (from default R)
optimx (from optimx R package)
GenSA (from GenSA R package)

...specifically, within each of these, a sub-algorithm is chosen that optimizes parameters within bounds (one of these is called L-BGFS-B, which if you google it you will see is an algorithm found in all sorts of implementations in various computer languages.

Each of these has a "stopping rule", which is something like "if the objective fails to improve by 0.00001 after x steps, then stop".  Sometimes the criterion is about the inferred slope of the objective (which will be 0 at the peak).  Usually there is an obscure way to change the default, but it is not trivial and requires burrowing into the original package (and sometimes the FORTRAN or C++ code underneath the R package).

Each optimizer returns a result which contains the maximized objective value, the parameters that produced this value, and some information on the search.  BioGeoBEARS just includes this whole output in the results object; to interpret it, you have to study the help for the original optimizer functions.

From faster to slower:
=============================
optimx with $speedup=TRUE
(the speedup=TRUE setting in BioGeoBEARS sets limits on the maximum number of iterations to search through)

optimx with $speedup=FALSE

optim

GenSA
=============================

In general, accuracy (meaning avoiding optimization failure, claiming a Max. Likelihood result that is a local optimum rather than the actual Maximum of the Likelihood) seems to work like this:
GenSA > optimx with $speedup=FALSE > optimx with $speedup=TRUE > optim

...but for most basic problems they all return the same thing.  The only place I've seen this trend matter in any reliable way is (1) very complex models (base models +x +traits etc.) or (2) weird cases with tiny datasets and 2 optima.

Therefore, if you have a particularly complex model, or just are worried, use GenSA (but it may take 2-10 times as long). 

Regardless, no optimizer is perfect, these are just hill-climbing algorithms of various sorts.  Advice:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#ML_optimx

In addition to the optimizer, the run time will be influenced by many other things:

More areas = more states/ranges = slower matrix exponentiation = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run
More free parameters = bigger parameter space to search through = slower overall run
Slower/older computer = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run

I was reading this thread and I have a question regarding the optimization/run time.

I've had in the past runs that were fast, average and slow.

What is the criteria the program uses to finish the run? How much does it need to converge/optimize? Is there a pre established criterion?

Cheers,

JP


Hi -- R has a large number of functions that do optimization (of likelihood or any other function that returns an objective that can be maximized or minimized).  There is a little world of such optimizers and math-type-people who construct them.

BioGeoBEARS allows 3 options:

optim (from default R)
optimx (from optimx R package)
GenSA (from GenSA R package)

...specifically, within each of these, a sub-algorithm is chosen that optimizes parameters within bounds (one of these is called L-BGFS-B, which if you google it you will see is an algorithm found in all sorts of implementations in various computer languages.

Each of these has a "stopping rule", which is something like "if the objective fails to improve by 0.00001 after x steps, then stop".  Sometimes the criterion is about the inferred slope of the objective (which will be 0 at the peak).  Usually there is an obscure way to change the default, but it is not trivial and requires burrowing into the original package (and sometimes the FORTRAN or C++ code underneath the R package).

Each optimizer returns a result which contains the maximized objective value, the parameters that produced this value, and some information on the search.  BioGeoBEARS just includes this whole output in the results object; to interpret it, you have to study the help for the original optimizer functions.


In general, speed works like this:

From faster to slower:
=============================
optimx with $speedup=TRUE
(the speedup=TRUE setting in BioGeoBEARS sets limits on the maximum number of iterations to search through)

optimx with $speedup=FALSE

optim

GenSA
=============================

In general, accuracy (meaning avoiding optimization failure, claiming a Max. Likelihood result that is a local optimum rather than the actual Maximum of the Likelihood) seems to work like this:
GenSA > optimx with $speedup=FALSE > optimx with $speedup=TRUE > optim

...but for most basic problems they all return the same thing.  The only place I've seen this trend matter in any reliable way is (1) very complex models (base models +x +traits etc.) or (2) weird cases with tiny datasets and 2 optima.

Therefore, if you have a particularly complex model, or just are worried, use GenSA (but it may take 2-10 times as long). 

Regardless, no optimizer is perfect, these are just hill-climbing algorithms of various sorts.  Advice:

ML optimization routines and their pitfalls
http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#ML_optimx


OTHER INFLUENCES ON RUN TIME

In addition to the optimizer, the run time will be influenced by many other things:

More areas = more states/ranges = slower matrix exponentiation = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run
More free parameters = bigger parameter space to search through = slower overall run
Slower/older computer = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run
Fewer cores / not using the multiple cores (R in Mac Terminal can do multicores, R.app cannot) = slower overall run

Cheers,
Nick

Before I look at details, **important** point here:

The goal with BioGeoBEARS, or any analysis, not to "get it to run".  The real goal is to understand what you are doing!!!!!  The current script has this for each model:

===================
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[1]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[2]] = states_list_0based_NEW

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[7]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[8]] = states_list_0based_NEW
===================

...this means you are time-stratifying the analysis, but each timeperiod has an identical list of states!  So, there is no reason to time-stratify. 

However, you get the same error with a non-time stratified analysis (lnL=-1e50 is equivalent to lnL=NaN), if the states_list is constrained.


OK, looking at your run:

1. The problem seems to be caused by the interaction between your user-constrained states_list and the DIVALIKE model. Between tips 2 and 3 (AB and BDE, tiplabels 1767 and 2359), the analysis can find no scenario that gives these tip data a nonzero probability at their common ancestor node. This is what failed:
nonadjacent=c("AC","AD","AE","AF","AG","AH","BE","BG","BH","CG","CH","DF","DG","DH","EH")

This, however, worked:
nonadjacent=c("AF","AG","AH","BG","BH","CG","CH","DF","DG","DH","EH")

...however, including AD, BE, etc. as disallowed ranges caused crashes again. So, these are crucial intermediate states for explaining sister species like (AB, BDE), under the DIVALIKE model. 


3.  HAVE A SERIOUS THINK ABOUT WHY YOU ARE CONSTRAINING ALLOWED RANGES AT ALL!  For example, you have a tip range of BDE.  All that is required to turn BDE into BE is an "e" event, loss of D.  So, how can BE really be considered an impossible range?  You have allowed everything up to ranges with a size of 4 areas, so eliminating a few 2-area ranges is a bit odd.


4. I have now updated the code so that an explicit error message is produced if the initial lnL calculation fails, and the run is stopped,.  Update from GitHub to get this fix.


5. On the other issues, you should really walk before you run!  In all things, the first steps are:

5a. Take a deep breath and review your decisions...does what your script is doing make sense?

5b. Do the same for whatever a reviewer says...reviewers often suggest things because they are mildly curious, that might make no difference.


6. "I have also tried o search for nay published paper using multiple Beast trees for the Biogeo analyses. but not seen any. Do you know of any such paper."

One of them is Wood, Matzke et al. 2012, Systematic Biology -- this was before BioGeoBEARS, but it ran Lagrange on a bunch of trees.  IMHO the effort-to-reward ratio was marginal in that case, but like I say here, it will all depend on how variable the BEAST trees are compared to the MCC tree: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/M8zw8Kidseo

Cheers,
Nick

Rscript myScript_v1.R

Rscript myScript_v1.R | tee screenoutput_v1.txt &

library(parallel)
...or...
library(snow)

...in your script. (It may be that both are required on your OS)


Cheers!
Nick
